soil-bio-196.title: Leaf mold, the slow fungal compost of autumn
soil-bio-196.text: A heap of autumn leaves can take one to three years to rot. Leaf mold is the compost that forms as fallen leaves decompose, mainly through slow, cool fungal breakdown rather than bacterial decay. The leaves are low in nitrogen and rich in cellulose and lignin, which resist decay. A succession of fungi, isopods, millipedes and earthworms turns them into fine, dark brown humic matter. In temperate deciduous woodland it slowly returns nutrients to plants. Poor in nutrients itself, it still improves soil, with a structure and moisture retention that suit seedling roots.

soil-bio-197.title: Coarse woody debris, the fallen trees that feed a forest
soil-bio-197.text: A fallen tree keeps working for centuries. Coarse woody debris means fallen dead trees and the remains of large branches lying in forests, rivers and wetlands. Authors set the minimum diameter anywhere from 2.5 to 20 cm. Saprotrophic fungi and detritivores consume it, recycling carbon, nitrogen, potassium and phosphorus. The wood is poor in nitrogen yet hosts free-living nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Fungi and other saprotrophs move its carbon into the soil, and in old-growth forests this storage can continue for hundreds of years. On slopes it slows the creep of organic matter and mineral soil, traps leaves, improves infiltration and slows evaporation.
